newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam to take advantage of coffee rally - trade.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam to take advantage of coffee rally - trade.

text.p: Vietnam is expected to try and take advantage of a sharp surge in international coffee prices to lock-in profits but may find it difficult to find buyers for its robusta beans, regional coffee traders said on Wednesday.

LIFFE coffee futures rallied strongly in London on Tuesday with the May contract hitting an intra-day high of US$1,680 a tonne before ending the day at $1,643. London prices have now risen by about 40 percent in the past month.
"I think Vietnam will definitely take advantage of the higher prices," a senior dealer at a European commodity trading house told Reuters.

"They will eventually benefit from these prices. Coffee is going to be the most volatile market over the next six months. You'll need a good daily dose of valium for this market," the chief coffee trader at another European trading house added.
"If the price in London holds above $1,640, we'll be in a new range for robusta coffee of $1,650-$1,850 a tonne. The old range was about $1,450-$1,650 (a tonne)," the trader added.
Prices For Vietnam's benchmark Grade 2, 8.0 percent black and broken, jumped up to around $1,300-$1,350 a tonne FOB Saigon against a quote last week of about $1,150-$1,230 a tonne, traders said.
But dealers said Vietnam may find it difficult to attract buyers as coffee roasters have stepped away from the market to wait for futures prices to ease.
"Vietnam can definitely sell at these levels, but the question is whether anybody will buy at these levels," one dealer said. "The roasters may wait for the prices to correct before coming in."

Most regional dealers expected London coffee futures to open lower later on Wednesday by around $10 a tonne, but in the longer term coffee prices are seen continuing to advance because of problems affecting the world's top two coffee producers -- Brazil and Colombia.

They said concerns over a smaller 1997/98 Brazilian crop, the approach of the southern hemisphere winter and potentially damaging frosts, a nationwide public workers strike in Colombia and generally tight supplies while the market awaits harvesting of the major Indonesian crop are factors underpinning prices.
"The long-term trend is up because of all those factors," one trader said.

On Tuesday, John Naranjo, commercial manager of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said he was unable to give an exact estimate of the extent to which the strike would delay exports. But he stressed that "the handling of coffee in ports has diminished."
"Colombia is a royal mess and it's so important for the coffee market," another dealer said.

Physical business in Vietnam remained slow as people drifted back from the long Tet Lunar New Year holidays, dealers said. "Most of the people still have hangovers. We'll only get to see some business being done probably next week," one commodity house dealer said.

Traders estimate that Vietnam has already sold about 150,000 tonnes of its robusta coffee crop. Most of the deals were done at around $1,000 a tonne FOB Saigon. About 100,000 to 120,000 tonnes remains to be sold, they said.
Congestion in the port of Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) remains a problem, the traders said.
"The congestion in Saigon is very, very bad," one said.
In Indonesia, most regional trading houses were undertaking surveys of the crop, where early harvesting begins in some areas in March.
"All these estimates about the crop being 15 percent down or 15 percent up is a lot of hot air. It's still too early to say how the crop will shape up," one trader said.
Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4 was indicated at around $1,400 a tonne FOB Panjang, traders said.

The robusta coffee contract on the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) was untraded on Tuesday. The price of the March contract was indicated at $1,553 a tonne. The market was closed on Monday for a holiday.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
